newsitem.title: IRAQ: No-fly zones aggressive, Clinton "retarded" - Iraq.
newsitem.headline: No-fly zones aggressive, Clinton "retarded" - Iraq.

text.p: Iraq on Sunday stepped up criticism of U.S. and allied no-fly zones over its territory, and one official newspaper described U.S. President Bill Clinton as "mentally retarded, immersed in vice and without conscience".
"The imposition of air exclusion zones in the north and south of our country is an aggressive measure by all standards," the ruling Baath party newspaper al-Thawra said in a front-page editorial.
It said the zones, policed by U.S. and allied planes, were "a dangerous precedent in international relations and conduct outside the framework of international legitimacy".
Thawra said the fight against the zones was "like the struggle between falsehood and truth", and Baghdad would decide how to counter violations of its airspace by allied warplanes.
Baghdad, in a bid to defuse the latest military crisis with the United States over the zones, announced on Friday that it would suspend missile attacks on intruding planes.

But it reiterated that this did not mean it recognised the zones, imposed after the 1991 Gulf War over Kuwait ostensibly to protect Kurds in the north and dissident Shi'ite Moslems in southern marshlands against possible attack by Iraqi forces.

The government newspaper al-Jumhouriya, which said on Saturday it hoped the decision to suspend missile attacks would ease tension in the Gulf, on Sunday attacked Clinton in some of the strongest language ever used by Iraq against a U.S. leader.
"He is mentally retarded, immersed in vice and without conscience," said a front-page editorial signed by editor-in-chief Salah al-Mukhtar.
"He shuddered and collapsed when (Republican presidential candidate Bob) Dole accused him of weakness in dealing with Iraq," Mukhtar said.
"The empire of evil in North America is the worst of its kind in history in terms of moral disgrace and degradation of human values," the paper said.

Clinton, who ordered two cruise missile attacks against Iraqi targets earlier this month, said on Saturday that the U.S. military had "tightened the strategic strait-jacket" on Iraqi President Saddam Hussein, one day after ordering more American troops to the Gulf.

Saddam on Saturday discussed with Defence Minister General Sultan Hashim Ahmed and senior officers from air defence units the redeployment of surface-to-air missiles to improve performance in case of another showdown with the United States.
Official newspapers said Saddam's youngest son, Qusay, overseeing operations of Iraq's elite Republican Guard, was also present. No further details were given.
The papers carried a front-page picture of Saddam meeting military aides and printed commentaries praising decisions taken by a meeting of Arab League foreign ministers in Cairo.

In the first formal resolution from the meeting, the ministers condemned Turkish, Iranian or any other intervention in northern Iraq and said a proposed Turkish buffer zone there would be a violation of Iraqi territory.
